Sharding means splitting your data across multiple database servers, so each server holds only a part of it. It might be necessary for these reasons: 1. Storage limits
Raw data for 1B URLs is only about 500 GB, which a single server can actually hold. But with indexes, replicas, metadata (click counts, expiry, user info), and growth over the years, it can reach several TB. At that point a single machine gets awkward and expensive. 2. Write throughput
One database server can only handle a limited number of writes per second. If creating links spikes (say, thousands of writes/sec at peak), one primary node becomes the bottleneck. Replication doesn't help here, because all writes still go to one primary. Sharding spreads writes across many primaries. 3.

Read throughput
Peak reads could be 3,000-6,000+ requests/second. A cache (Redis) absorbs most of it, but cache misses still hit the database. Replicas help with reads, but sharding gives more total capacity. 4. Memory and index size
Fast lookups need indexes to fit in RAM. If the index for 1B keys is bigger than one server's memory, lookups get slow. Sharded, each server's index is smaller and fits in memory. 5. Availability and blast radius
If one huge database fails, everything is down. With shards, a failure affects only part of the data (and each shard can have its own replicas). Honest note: at 1B URLs, sharding is not strictly required on day one. Many real systems start with one primary and several read replicas plus a cache, and shard later.

In an interview, a good answer is: "Storage fits on one machine, but I'd shard for write throughput, growth, and availability." How you'd shard: hash the short code (e.g., hash(short_code) % N, or better, consistent hashing) so data spreads evenly and a lookup goes straight to the right shard.
